rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more usable routing: four real desks, four protagonists, and proof gates that would stop a lazy blast before it leaves the building. Its best line, "Monzo's second US attempt starts invite-only, without the banking license it failed to get last time," is a real banking-trade story with teeth. B is good, but calling "Exclusive: inside Monzo's invite-only US launch" a "duplicate" throws away a viable consumer-finance access story; that's not discipline, that's leaving a pitchable lane on the floor.
gaps_in_A: "Nine million UK customers, zero in the US" overstates the record. The update says the US launch is invite-only and a prior attempt was abandoned; it does not prove zero current or prior US customers.
"then immediately spent it on the market" implies the UK profit funded the US expansion. The facts establish sequence, not financing or causality, and CAC/US targets are explicitly undisclosed.
"it won't let most people open" is directionally fair from invite-only, but "most" needs allocation numbers. Without invite volume, it is a sharp consumer line sitting on a thin fact.
gaps_in_B: "how the US entry playbook has changed" is bigger than the supplied facts. B has one Monzo before-and-after, not evidence that the wider playbook changed.
"then spent it on a second shot at America" makes the same financing leap A makes. B wisely warns not to infer the profit link, then lets the headline infer it anyway.

"the invite-only detail is texture inside the market-test angle, not a separate story" is too dismissive. Access terms, waitlist mechanics, FDIC setup, fees, and availability are exactly what a US consumer-money desk can cover.

The proof asks are thinner than A's. The first angle asks for the partner bank name but not deposit-insurance structure, customer relationship ownership, fee control, or regulatory exposure, which are the bones of the story.
